conceptTag: Alfred Sloan's divisions at General Motors
readerTitle: How General Motors beat Ford by splitting itself into divisions
caseNote: 실제 기업 (General Motors, Ford, 1920년대 재편과 이후 브랜드 정리) + 실제 연구 (Chandler 1962) + 가상 적용 (호텔 그룹)
insight: 분권이 잘 되려면 중앙이 일을 덜 하는 것이 아니라 다른 일을 해야 한다. 사업부에 운영을 맡기고, 중앙은 각 사업부의 영역을 정하고 같은 기준으로 성과를 재고 큰 돈을 배분한다.
misconception: 조직 구조는 중앙집권과 분권 중 하나를 고르는 문제다. 사업부에 자율을 주면 중앙은 손을 떼면 된다.

sources.text: Sloan, A. P. (1963). My Years with General Motors. Doubleday. (1920년 위기, Organization Study, 1921년 제품 정책과 가격대 구분, 'coordinated decentralization' 개념)
Chandler, A. D. (1962). Strategy and Structure: Chapters in the History of the American Industrial Enterprise. MIT Press. (GM과 DuPont의 사업부제 도입 사례)
Drucker, P. F. (1946). Concept of the Corporation. John Day. (GM 사업부 구조 연구)
General Motors 발표: Oldsmobile 단계적 폐지(2000년 발표, 2004년 종료), Pontiac 폐지(2009년 발표, 2010년 종료)
호텔 그룹 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Durant의 퇴진(1920년 11월), Pierre S. du Pont의 사장 취임, Sloan의 Organization Study 채택, Sloan의 사장 취임(1923년)을 Sloan(1963)과 Chandler(1962)로 확인하세요.
'GM이 1920년대 말까지 Ford를 제치고 미국 최대 자동차 회사가 되었다'는 표현은 연도별 판매 자료로 확인이 필요합니다. 정확한 연도와 점유율 수치는 일부러 쓰지 않았습니다.
1921년 제품 정책에서 가격 사다리(Chevrolet 최저가부터 Cadillac 최고가까지)와 겹치는 가격대 정리를 다뤘습니다. 당시 Pontiac은 Oakland 사업부였으므로 카드에서는 Pontiac 이름을 쓰지 않았습니다. 사다리의 브랜드 순서를 다시 확인하세요.
'coordinated decentralization'은 Sloan이 쓴 표현으로 널리 인용됩니다. 원문 인용이 아니라 개념 이름으로만 썼습니다. My Years with General Motors에서 표현을 확인하세요.
이후 브랜드 간 부품·디자인 공유가 늘어 차들이 비슷해졌다는 비판(1980년대)은 널리 기록된 내용이지만 정성적으로만 서술했습니다. Oldsmobile과 Pontiac 폐지 연도를 GM 발표로 확인하세요.

cards.title: How General Motors beat Ford by splitting itself into divisions
body: In 1920, General Motors owned Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, Oldsmobile and more. Several of its cars chased the same buyers at similar prices.
Ford, run tightly from the top, sold far more cars than any rival. Then a recession hit, and GM nearly came apart.
Its answer was not more control or less control. It was a new kind of control.

image.label: Several car factories pulling in different directions
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1920년대풍 자동차 공장 다섯 채가 각자 다른 방향으로 밧줄을 당기고, 가운데 작은 본사 건물이 흔들리는 장면. 실제 자동차 브랜드 로고와 엠블럼은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 1920. How do you organize GM?
body: GM is a loose group of carmakers. Each division plans its own cars, prices and spending. Some compete for the same customers. Head office can barely see what each one spends until the bills arrive.
Ford, your big rival, runs one car from one central office. What do you do?

options.text: Centralize: one head office runs design, production and sales for every brand
options.feedback: You gain control, but one office can't make fast, informed calls for several different car businesses. You'd also sideline the managers who know their markets best.

options.text: Let each division run itself, but have the center set price lanes, compare results and approve big spending
options.feedback: Divisions keep speed and ownership. The center stops them colliding and sees trouble early. This is close to what GM did.

options.text: Keep divisions fully independent and let the strongest ones win
options.feedback: You keep energy and local knowledge. But divisions keep fighting over the same buyers, and nobody spots overspending until it's too late.

cards.title: Alfred Sloan's plan
body: GM's founder, William Durant, left in late 1920. The new leadership under Pierre du Pont adopted a plan written by a GM executive, **Alfred Sloan**, who became president in 1923.

Each division got a general manager responsible for its own engineering, production and sales. A small central office handled finance, policy and research, and required every division to report results the same way.
In 1921, GM also gave each division its own price range, from Chevrolet at the bottom to Cadillac at the top. Overlaps were cut.

cards.title: Coordinated decentralization
body: **Coordinated decentralization** means pushing day-to-day decisions down to the units that run the business, while the center keeps a few jobs no unit can do alone.
At GM, the center did three things: it drew the lanes each division ran in, measured every division with the same numbers, and decided where big money went. Everything else belonged to the divisions.

image.label: A price ladder with one car brand on each rung
image.brief: 가격 사다리 인포그래픽. 아래 칸 "Lowest price"부터 위 칸 "Highest price"까지 칸마다 다른 모양의 자동차 실루엣. 사다리 옆에 작은 본사 건물이 "Lanes · Numbers · Money" 세 개의 라벨을 들고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A software company with several product teams faces the same split. Teams can own their roadmaps, but someone must decide which customers each product serves, track every team on the same metrics, and set headcount budgets.

cards.title: A car for every buyer, not one car for all.
body: Ford built its success on the Model T, one car made ever cheaper. As buyers grew richer, many wanted more choice and newer styles.
GM's divisions could each serve a different kind of buyer, and customers could trade up the ladder over time. By the end of the 1920s, GM had passed Ford as America's largest carmaker.
Historian Alfred Chandler later studied GM and DuPont in *Strategy and Structure* (1962). The multi-division design he described spread to many large companies.

cards.title: The lanes need guarding.
body: Coordination is ongoing work. Over later decades, GM divisions shared more parts and designs to save money. Critics, especially in the 1980s, said many GM cars looked alike across brands.
Once the lanes blurred, divisions again competed for the same buyers. GM ended Oldsmobile in 2004 and Pontiac in 2010.
Decentralization does not run itself. If the center stops defining lanes, the structure slowly turns back into the mess it replaced.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel group.
body: You own three hotels in one city: a budget hotel, a mid-range hotel and a luxury hotel. Each has its own manager. Lately the luxury hotel discounts into mid-range prices, and the mid-range hotel undercuts the budget one. Total profit is falling.
What do you change?

options.text: Replace the three managers with one manager who sets every price and policy
options.feedback: The price war ends, but one person now runs three very different guest experiences. You lose fast local decisions and managers who own their results.

options.text: Keep each manager in charge, but set a price range per hotel and judge each on its own profit
options.feedback: Managers keep running their hotels. The center draws the lanes and measures fairly, so winning means serving your own guests better, not taking a sister hotel's.

options.text: Pay every manager a bonus on the group's total profit
options.feedback: Shared bonuses can reduce poaching. But without clear lanes, each manager still lacks a clear target, and strong performers carry weak ones.

cards.title: Give units the running. Keep the lanes, the numbers and the money.
body: Sloan's lesson isn't "decentralize." It's that freedom works when the center defines who each unit serves, measures every unit the same way, and decides where big investments go.
**Try it today:** list your teams or locations. For each, write the one customer group it owns. Where two teams share the same answer, you have a lane to redraw.
